title: Not a programmer, but I know what I want – how I made a full idle game with my sons and three AIs (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini + Suno music)
author: Seboklarus133
selftext:
I'm a dad from Poland. I'm not a programmer, but I'm not completely lost either – I can read what's going on, test everything myself and catch a lot of bugs on my own. What I bring is the vision: I know exactly what the game should be, how it should look and feel, and what should happen on the screen. The AI does the heavy lifting with the code.

Over the last few weeks I made Fern Flower, a cozy idle game based on Slavic folklore (chop an enchanted forest, rebuild a village, fight the Leshy, find the fern flower on Kupala Night). It's free on itch.io, and I wanted to share how I work, because it took a lot of trial and error.

Ideas come from the whole family. My sons are my testers and my design team – I ask them what they would want in the game, what's fun and what's boring, and a lot of features came straight from them. Then I do a kind of brainstorm with three AIs: I give the same idea to ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini and ask how they see it – what's possible, what's easy, what's hard, what could break. Comparing their answers helps me pick a version that actually works, before anything gets built.

The code is Godot 4, written by Claude. At first the whole game was one huge file and every new feature broke something else. What fixed it was asking the AI to split everything into small modules and to write automatic tests – now after every change it runs a test that plays through the whole story and takes screenshots of every window. That catches most bugs before my sons (the testers) find them.

The second big thing was memory between chats. The AI forgets everything, so I keep a notes file with the current state of the project, and every chat updates it. Without that I was explaining the same things over and over.

The art is ChatGPT images. Characters and buildings I ask for as sprite sheets, then they get cut into separate pieces. Keeping the same style was the hardest part – I always attach 1–2 earlier images as a reference.

The music is 8 tracks from Suno, and the game crossfades between them depending on where you are: forest by day, fireflies at night, the village fair, a boss fight, Kupala Night.

Not everything went well: one big portal rejected the game for "quality", and my own anti-theft lock once blocked me from playing my own game on my phone :)

Play free (browser, Android, Windows, Linux): https://seboklarusbiuro.itch.io/kwiat-paproci  
Trailer: https://youtu.be/0hru9cqCuyE?is=Km0h7QfnrHGlG30y

I'm curious how others keep a consistent art style with image models – any tricks?
